title: The House of Wisdom
hook: a Baghdad center where scholars translated and studied Greek, Persian and Indian works

segments.voice: Yesterday, Harun al-Rashid: the caliph of the tales and the ruler of the histories. Your line was: legend and history. Which story did you sort into its two piles? Day nine hundred fifteen.

A caliph dreams that a man is sitting on his bed: fair-skinned and broad-browed. The caliph asks who he is. Aristotle, the man says. The caliph asks him, what is good? The dream-Aristotle answers in steps: first, whatever reason finds good; then, whatever the religious law finds good; then, whatever people find good. That is a story the bookseller Ibn al-Nadim tells about the caliph al-Ma'mun, Harun's son, as one reason Greek books were sought out and brought to Baghdad. Whether or not the dream happened, the books really came, and something in Baghdad took them in. It had a name: Bayt al-Hikmah. Today: the House of Wisdom.
screen: `A CALIPH'S DREAM.` → `WHAT IS GOOD?` → `BOOKS BROUGHT TO BAGHDAD.`

segments.voice: Bayt al-Hikmah means the House of Wisdom. Start with a caution: historians argue about what it actually was. A palace library? A translation office? A meeting place for scholars? The sources are thin, and it may have been smaller than its fame. What isn't in doubt is the work done in Baghdad in those generations. Books in Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit were turned into Arabic: Euclid's geometry, Ptolemy's astronomy, the medicine of Galen, the philosophy of Aristotle, Persian wisdom literature, Indian astronomy and numbers. The people doing the work were not all Muslims. One well-known translator, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, was a Christian physician. In a letter he wrote about his work, he describes hunting for several copies of a book by Galen and comparing them before he translated, because copies differ and mistakes creep in. A later writer, al-Safadi, describes his way as carrying over the meaning of a whole sentence, not swapping word for word. Muslim scholars took up these books, argued with them, corrected them and built on them, in mathematics, medicine and philosophy. Why would a Muslim court spend so much on foreign books? Some readers point to the Qur'an, which says God gives wisdom to whom He wills, and that whoever is given wisdom has been given much good. Wisdom, on that view, isn't owned by one people. It's a gift you go looking for. Wisdom from everywhere.
screen: `WHAT WAS IT, REALLY?` · `GREEK, PERSIAN, INDIAN, INTO ARABIC.` · `HUNAYN COMPARES THE COPIES.` · then, large: `WISDOM IS A GIFT TO SEEK.`

segments.voice: The practice: read something translated. Before you look anything up, sit and breathe. Bring to mind one book, poem or text you've read that was written in another language. A novel, a scripture, a set of instructions, a song lyric. Breathe in. Someone carried those words across for you: a translator whose name you may not know. Breathe out. Give them a moment of thanks. After the sit, read a few lines of something translated, slowly, the way Hunayn read Galen, with care for what the writer meant. If you pray, you can ask in your own words to recognize wisdom wherever it turns up. The bell holds the time.
Bayt al-Hikmah. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad, linked with the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Today's word.
Your line: wisdom from everywhere. Today, learn one good thing from someone you wouldn't usually listen to. Day nine hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars point to the House of Wisdom and the translation movement when they talk about learning from other peoples, and historians study the surviving Arabic translations and Hunayn's own letter about his work.
